Introduction¶

In this project, we will investigate which audio features of a song can be used to predict a song's popularity. Below is a table of all the features included in the data set.

Feature Description Range / Unit
Popularity Spotify popularity score 0–100
Danceability Suitability for dancing 0–1
Energy Intensity and activity of the track 0–1
Loudness Average loudness Decibels (dB)
Speechiness Presence of spoken words 0–1
Acousticness Likelihood that the track is acoustic 0–1
Instrumentalness Likelihood that the track has no vocals 0–1
Liveness Likelihood of a live recording 0–1
Valence Musical positivity or happiness 0–1
Tempo Speed of the track Beats per minute (BPM)
Duration Length of the track Milliseconds
Key Estimated musical key 0–11
Mode Major or minor mode 0 or 1
Time Signature Estimated beats per measure Integer

| Explicitness | Contains explicit lyrics | True/False

For our research question, the features we will use for our analysis include: danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, and tempo. Popularity is based off of total number of plays a track has and how recent those plays are. The initial data set has 114000 entries.

# load in data
data = pd.read_csv('/content/drive/MyDrive/Colab/math237/data/dataset.csv')

Cleaning¶

Before we begin our analysis, we first take out songs with duplicate entries and songs with missing values. There is only one song with missing columns. It has a track ID, but no name, artist, or popularity. Therefore we will remove the song from our data. There are 24,259 songs with duplicate track ID's in our dataset. We will also drop these songs to prevent repeated entries from disproportionately affecting our analysis.

# find rows with missing values
rows_with_nan = data[data.isna().any(axis=1)]
print(rows_with_nan)
# drop missing row and duplicates
my_spot = data.drop(index=rows_with_nan.index)
my_spot = my_spot.drop_duplicates(subset=['track_id']).copy()
# how many songs removed
n_diff = len(data) - len(my_spot)
print(f'Removed {n_diff} songs.')

Aside from missing data and duplicate ID's, we noticed that there was a high amount songs with a popularity score of 0,1, and 2. There are two explanations for this. The first is that these songs were recently uploaded to spotify at the time of data collection and have not had the time to gather plays. The second is because some songs show up multiple times, yet have different track ID's. This is because they are apart of "collection albums," which are essentially a playlist of songs that are under the same category. The songs in these albums tend to have a much lower score than the song uploaded by the original artist, so we remove them from the data to get a better estimation of our features.

Feature Engineering¶

Apart from cleaning the data, we also decided to split the songs into different bins of based off popularity. This will allow us to further investigate audio features across songs with low, medium, and high popularity. We based our cutoffs on the interquartile range to insure we have a proportionate amount of samples in each bin

my_spot['Pop_level'] = pd.cut(
    my_spot['popularity'],
    bins = [-1,30,44,100],
    labels = ['Low', 'Medium', 'High']
)

Initial Statistics¶

Now that we have cleaned the data, we can start the initial analysis of our dataset. Across the entire dataset, the mean popularity is 37.823 with a standard deviation of 17.573. From the histogram, we can see that the popularity of songs is somewhat normally distributed across the range of 0-100.

#histogram with popularity on x-axis and amount on y-axis
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.hist(my_spot['popularity'], bins=15, color='skyblue', alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')
plt.title('Distribution of Popularity', fontsize=16)
plt.xlabel('Popularity', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Number of songs', fontsize=12)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

print(f"Across all songs, the median popularity is {my_spot['popularity'].median()} with a mean of {my_spot['popularity'].mean()}.")

print(f"Across all songs, the standard deviation is {my_spot['popularity'].std()}.")

Across all songs, the median popularity is 37.0 with a mean of 37.82330745874252.
Across all songs, the standard deviation is 17.573305788343323.

We also find the mean and standard deviation across all audio features we are investigating. One thing to note, since most of these features range from 0-1, we can see that some features have relatively high deviation. Notably, energy, accousticness, instrumentalness, and valence all have higher deviations.

audio_features = [
    'danceability', 'energy', 'loudness', 'speechiness',
    'valence', 'liveness', 'instrumentalness', 'acousticness',
]
# standard deviation for audio features
mu = my_spot[audio_features].mean()
std_dev = my_spot[audio_features].std()
# print features with mean and sd as table (0 = mean, 1 = sd)
print(pd.concat([mu, std_dev], axis=1))

Scatter Plots¶

We plot each audio feature on the x-axis and popularity on the y-axis to visualize the relationship between them. We can use these to identify some pattern across the variables. While its hard to see the correlation between features and popularity, we can see some clusters form in the graphs. In the Speechiness graph, we can see that there is a small cluster of songs that have high speechiness and low popularity.

# plot each audio feature on the x-axis with popularity on the y-axis
audio_features = [
    'danceability', 'energy', 'loudness', 'speechiness',
    'valence', 'liveness', 'instrumentalness', 'acousticness',
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(18, 10))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, feature in enumerate(audio_features):
    axes[i].scatter(my_spot[feature], my_spot['popularity'], alpha=0.5)
    axes[i].set_xlabel(feature, fontsize=1)
    axes[i].set_ylabel('Popularity', fontsize=1)
    axes[i].set_title(f'{feature} vs. Popularity', fontsize=12)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Correlation Heat Map¶

We use a heatmap to visualize the correlations between each audio feature and popularity. While there are no features that have a high, positive correlation with popularity, we can see that some features have a high, positive correlation with each other. Notably, energy and loudness have a high correlation as well as danceability and valence. However, there are audio features with a negative correlation with positivity, those being instrumentalness and speechiness.

categorical_features = [
    'popularity', 'danceability', 'energy', 'loudness', 'speechiness',
    'valence', 'liveness', 'instrumentalness', 'acousticness',
]



# Calculate the correlation matrix
corr_matrix = my_spot[categorical_features].corr()

# Generate the heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(
    corr_matrix,
    annot=True,
    cmap='coolwarm',
    fmt='.2f',
    linewidths=0.5,
    vmin=-1,
    vmax=1
)
plt.title('Correlation of Audio Features', fontsize=14, pad=15)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

We can already see the difference in popularity mean across genre compared to the mean of popularity across all songs is high.

Correlation Heat Maps¶

We will use heat maps to visualize correlation across audio features by genre. We can see that some genres differ in which features correlate with higher popularity. For example, we can see that speechiness has a positive correlation with popularity for soul music, but a negative correlation with popularity for electro music.

# correlation matrix for each genre
corr_matrix_electro = electro[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_rock = rock[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_pop = pop[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_soul = soul[categorical_features].corr()
corr_matrix_house = house[categorical_features].corr()

genres = ['electro', 'pop', 'rock', 'soul', 'house']

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 10))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, genre in enumerate(genres):
    corr_matrix = globals()[f'corr_matrix_{genre}']

    sns.heatmap(
        corr_matrix,
        annot=True,
        cmap='coolwarm',
        fmt='.2f',
        linewidths=0.5,
        vmin=-1,
        vmax=1,
        ax=axes[i],
        cbar=False
    )

    axes[i].set_title(f'Correlation for {genre}', fontsize=12, pad=10)

# remove unused sixth subplot
fig.delaxes(axes[5])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Discussion¶

We can separate these music genres into accoustic (soul, pop, rock) and synthesized (house, electro) music. We create these groups to distinguish the fact that different features correlate with higher popularity. A common factor across the accoustic group is that speechiness correlates positively with popularity. We can infer that the presence of lyrics is important for these genres. Accousticness is also a feature that correlates positively with popularity. This highlights the importance of sound created by instruments rather than synthesized music in these genres. For the synthesized group, we can see that the feature is slightly favored is liveness. This means that the songs that are most popular in these genres are songs that were performed live. One interesting thing to note, is that the electro genre's features do not highly correlate with popularity at all. This could be mean that there are some outside factors that drive this genre to popularity, like cultural trends or the artist who composed the song.

Features By Genre with Popularity Bins¶

The bar chart was created with the facet_wrap function to compare numbers of songs across different music genres based on their popularity levels. By separating low, medium, and high popularity levels into individual panels which compare the distribution of songs.

Based from 'Numbers of songs by Genre and Popularity' graph helps identify which music genres have more songs classified. Low score is (0-30), medium is (31-44) and high is (45-100). In the high popularity category, ambient has 671 songs followed with acoustic at 559 songs and alt rock with 521 songs. In contrast, tango has the highest numbers of low-popularity songs, with 967 songs then there's Chicago-house second highest with 922 songs. As for the medium-popularity category, forro has the highest number of songs which are 779 songs, followed by study at 349 songs.

The bar graph shows how song popularity varies across different music genres. The graph shows that certain genres, such as ambient, acoustic, and alt rock have large numbers of highly popular songs while tango,chicago and bluegrass contain more songs but with low popularity scores. These differences suggesst a possible association between music genre and song popularity. However, because the graph displays song counts rather than percentages, it cannot determine which genres have the highest proportion of popular songs

top_genres = my_spot['track_genre'].value_counts().head(10).index

spotify_top10 = my_spot[my_spot['track_genre'].isin(top_genres)]

(
    ggplot(spotify_top10)
    + geom_bar(aes(x = 'track_genre', fill = 'Pop_level'), position= 'dodge')
    + labs(
        title = 'Numbers of songs by Genre and Popularity',
        x = 'Music Genre',
        y = 'Number of Songs',
        fill = 'Popularity Level'
    )

    + facet_wrap('Pop_level')


)

The grouped bar chart was created to see the relationship between music genre and song popularity by comparing the percentage of songs classified as having low, medium, or high popularity. The visualization uses percentages to show differences in the total number of songs within each genre which will make meaningful comparisons and identify which genres have a greater proportion of popular songs

Based on the grouped bar chart, the x axis represents the different music genres,while the Y-axis represents the percentage of songs within each popularity category. The output shows ambient has the highest percentage of high percentage of highly popular songs at 67%, followed by acoustic at 56% and alt-rock at 52%. In contrast, tango has 97% percent of its songs labeled as low popularity, then Chicago-house at 92% and bluegrass at 87% in the same category. As for the medium category, forro has the highest percentage at 78%. These insights show music genres associated with song popularity, as some genres have a much higher proportion of popular songs than others.

The visualization shows the distribution of song popularity differs across music genres. The visualization uses percentages to make comparisons across genres regardless of their total count.

genre_percent = (
    spotify_top10
    .groupby(['track_genre', 'Pop_level'], observed=True)
    .size()
    .reset_index(name='count')
)

genre_percent['percentage'] = (
    genre_percent['count']
    / genre_percent.groupby('track_genre')['count'].transform('sum')
    * 100
)
(
    ggplot(genre_percent)
    + geom_bar(
      aes(
            x='track_genre',
            y='percentage',
            fill='Pop_level'
        ),
        stat='identity',
        position='dodge'
    )
    +labs(
        title='Percentage of Popularity Levels by Genre',
        x='Music Genre',
        y='Percentage of Songs (%)',
        fill='Popularity Level'
    )
    + scale_y_continuous(
        breaks=[0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100],
        limits=[0, 100]
    )
    + theme(
        axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1)
    )
    + ggsize(900, 600)
)

This application is used to convert notebook files (*.ipynb)

Options
=======
The options below are convenience aliases to configurable class-options,
as listed in the "Equivalent to" description-line of the aliases.
To see all configurable class-options for some <cmd>, use:
    <cmd> --help-all

--debug
    set log level to logging.DEBUG (maximize logging output)
    Equivalent to: [--Application.log_level=10]
--show-config
    Show the application's configuration (human-readable format)
    Equivalent to: [--Application.show_config=True]
--show-config-json
    Show the application's configuration (json format)
    Equivalent to: [--Application.show_config_json=True]
--generate-config
    generate default config file
    Equivalent to: [--JupyterApp.generate_config=True]
-y
    Answer yes to any questions instead of prompting.
    Equivalent to: [--JupyterApp.answer_yes=True]
--execute
    Execute the notebook prior to export.
    Equivalent to: [--ExecutePreprocessor.enabled=True]
--allow-errors
    Continue notebook execution even if one of the cells throws an error and include the error message in the cell output (the default behaviour is to abort conversion). This flag is only relevant if '--execute' was specified, too.
    Equivalent to: [--ExecutePreprocessor.allow_errors=True]
--stdin
    read a single notebook file from stdin. Write the resulting notebook with default basename 'notebook.*'
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.from_stdin=True]
--stdout
    Write notebook output to stdout instead of files.
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.writer_class=StdoutWriter]
--inplace
    Run nbconvert in place, overwriting the existing notebook (only
            relevant when converting to notebook format)
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.use_output_suffix=False --NbConvertApp.export_format=notebook --FilesWriter.build_directory=]
--clear-output
    Clear output of current file and save in place,
            overwriting the existing notebook.
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.use_output_suffix=False --NbConvertApp.export_format=notebook --FilesWriter.build_directory= --ClearOutputPreprocessor.enabled=True]
--coalesce-streams
    Coalesce consecutive stdout and stderr outputs into one stream (within each cell).
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.use_output_suffix=False --NbConvertApp.export_format=notebook --FilesWriter.build_directory= --CoalesceStreamsPreprocessor.enabled=True]
--no-prompt
    Exclude input and output prompts from converted document.
    Equivalent to: [--TemplateExporter.exclude_input_prompt=True --TemplateExporter.exclude_output_prompt=True]
--no-input
    Exclude input cells and output prompts from converted document.
            This mode is ideal for generating code-free reports.
    Equivalent to: [--TemplateExporter.exclude_output_prompt=True --TemplateExporter.exclude_input=True --TemplateExporter.exclude_input_prompt=True]
--allow-chromium-download
    Whether to allow downloading chromium if no suitable version is found on the system.
    Equivalent to: [--WebPDFExporter.allow_chromium_download=True]
--disable-chromium-sandbox
    Disable chromium security sandbox when converting to PDF..
    Equivalent to: [--WebPDFExporter.disable_sandbox=True]
--show-input
    Shows code input. This flag is only useful for dejavu users.
    Equivalent to: [--TemplateExporter.exclude_input=False]
--embed-images
    Embed the images as base64 dataurls in the output. This flag is only useful for the HTML/WebPDF/Slides exports.
    Equivalent to: [--HTMLExporter.embed_images=True]
--sanitize-html
    Whether the HTML in Markdown cells and cell outputs should be sanitized..
    Equivalent to: [--HTMLExporter.sanitize_html=True]
--log-level=<Enum>
    Set the log level by value or name.
    Choices: any of [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 'DEBUG', 'INFO', 'WARN', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL']
    Default: 30
    Equivalent to: [--Application.log_level]
--config=<Unicode>
    Full path of a config file.
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--JupyterApp.config_file]
--to=<Unicode>
    The export format to be used, either one of the built-in formats
            ['asciidoc', 'custom', 'html', 'latex', 'markdown', 'notebook', 'pdf', 'python', 'qtpdf', 'qtpng', 'rst', 'script', 'slides', 'webpdf']
            or a dotted object name that represents the import path for an
            ``Exporter`` class
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.export_format]
--template=<Unicode>
    Name of the template to use
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--TemplateExporter.template_name]
--template-file=<Unicode>
    Name of the template file to use
    Default: None
    Equivalent to: [--TemplateExporter.template_file]
--theme=<Unicode>
    Template specific theme(e.g. the name of a JupyterLab CSS theme distributed
    as prebuilt extension for the lab template)
    Default: 'light'
    Equivalent to: [--HTMLExporter.theme]
--sanitize_html=<Bool>
    Whether the HTML in Markdown cells and cell outputs should be sanitized.This
    should be set to True by nbviewer or similar tools.
    Default: False
    Equivalent to: [--HTMLExporter.sanitize_html]
--writer=<DottedObjectName>
    Writer class used to write the
                                        results of the conversion
    Default: 'FilesWriter'
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.writer_class]
--post=<DottedOrNone>
    PostProcessor class used to write the
                                        results of the conversion
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.postprocessor_class]
--output=<Unicode>
    Overwrite base name use for output files.
                Supports pattern replacements '{notebook_name}'.
    Default: '{notebook_name}'
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.output_base]
--output-dir=<Unicode>
    Directory to write output(s) to. Defaults
                                  to output to the directory of each notebook. To recover
                                  previous default behaviour (outputting to the current
                                  working directory) use . as the flag value.
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--FilesWriter.build_directory]
--reveal-prefix=<Unicode>
    The URL prefix for reveal.js (version 3.x).
            This defaults to the reveal CDN, but can be any url pointing to a copy
            of reveal.js.
            For speaker notes to work, this must be a relative path to a local
            copy of reveal.js: e.g., "reveal.js".
            If a relative path is given, it must be a subdirectory of the
            current directory (from which the server is run).
            See the usage documentation
            (https://nbconvert.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage.html#reveal-js-html-slideshow)
            for more details.
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--SlidesExporter.reveal_url_prefix]
--nbformat=<Enum>
    The nbformat version to write.
            Use this to downgrade notebooks.
    Choices: any of [1, 2, 3, 4]
    Default: 4
    Equivalent to: [--NotebookExporter.nbformat_version]

Examples
--------

    The simplest way to use nbconvert is

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to html

            Options include ['asciidoc', 'custom', 'html', 'latex', 'markdown', 'notebook', 'pdf', 'python', 'qtpdf', 'qtpng', 'rst', 'script', 'slides', 'webpdf'].

            > jupyter nbconvert --to latex mynotebook.ipynb

            Both HTML and LaTeX support multiple output templates. LaTeX includes
            'base', 'article' and 'report'.  HTML includes 'basic', 'lab' and
            'classic'. You can specify the flavor of the format used.

            > jupyter nbconvert --to html --template lab mynotebook.ipynb

            You can also pipe the output to stdout, rather than a file

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --stdout

            PDF is generated via latex

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to pdf

            You can get (and serve) a Reveal.js-powered slideshow

            > jupyter nbconvert myslides.ipynb --to slides --post serve

            Multiple notebooks can be given at the command line in a couple of
            different ways:

            > jupyter nbconvert notebook*.ipynb
            > jupyter nbconvert notebook1.ipynb notebook2.ipynb

            or you can specify the notebooks list in a config file, containing::

                c.NbConvertApp.notebooks = ["my_notebook.ipynb"]

            > jupyter nbconvert --config mycfg.py

To see all available configurables, use `--help-all`.
